title: The Half-Light Wardrobe
premise: Ulyana Delacroix has spent fifteen years writing postcards to his family's burned-down house, a ritual that lets him confess everything to no one. When the charred lot is auctioned off, he returns to claim—or sabotage—the sale, only to find his estranged sister Vivienne bidding against him and an untranslated sentence in their late mother's handwriting hidden in the wardrobe frame that survived the fire. As the auction deadline collides with the final bus route to the old neighborhood, Ulyana must finally translate the sentence—'I knew what he did, and I stayed'—and decide whether inheritance means keeping secrets or burning them openly. He loses the house but gains the truth, mailing his last postcard with a return address for the first time.
about_author: Juniper Zhou is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing unclaimed letters in municipal storage. Their fiction explores what families preserve when they cannot bear to remember.

chapters.title: Postcards to Ash
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. We meet him writing his weekly postcard to an address that no longer exists, his apartment a museum of unsent drafts. A legal letter arrives: the Delacroix lot enters auction in six weeks. Emotional beat: quiet dread disguised as routine, the first crack in his carefully maintained invisibility.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV, flashback-woven. He catalogs his family's silences—his father's rages, his mother's complicity, Vivienne's flight—in a notebook he treats as scripture. He learns Vivienne has hired a lawyer too. Emotional beat: the realization that his sister has been keeping her own inventory all along.

chapters.title: Bus 44, Last Stop
chapters.summary: Vivienne's POV. She rides the soon-to-be-rerouted Bus 44 back toward the neighborhood she escaped at nineteen, rehearsing arguments for why she should win the auction. She remembers the night of the fire differently than Ulyana does. Emotional beat: grief braided with ambition; she wants the land not as memorial but as erasure.

chapters.title: What Survived the Fire
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. Visiting the fenced lot before the auction, he finds the iron wardrobe frame half-buried, and inside its hollow rail, a rolled paper in his mother's hand—one sentence, in a language neither sibling speaks fluently. Emotional beat: vertigo; the past was never ash, only buried.

chapters.title: Bidding Wars
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The siblings collide at a pre-auction open house, trading barbed courtesies while a developer circles like weather. Ulyana conceals the paper; Vivienne reveals she knows about it. Emotional beat: power shifting between them, each discovering the other's leverage.

chapters.title: The Translator's Fee
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. He hires Marisol, an aging translator who refuses payment until she understands why the sentence matters. Her questions force him closer to confession than any postcard ever did. Emotional beat: intimacy through interrogation; being seen feels like drowning and breathing at once.

chapters.title: Vivienne's Version
chapters.summary: Vivienne's POV. She confronts Ulyana with her memory of the fire—that their mother set it deliberately, and that Ulyana watched and said nothing. The accusation lands on the exact wound the sentence gestures toward. Emotional beat: betrayal curdling into recognition; both were children guarding the same crime.

chapters.title: The Sentence
chapters.summary: Marisol delivers the translation: 'I knew what he did, and I stayed.' Ulyana reads it aloud alone in his apartment, then burns every postcard except one. Emotional beat: climax of interiority—the untranslatable made plain, and the terrible freedom of no longer being able to hide behind language.

chapters.title: Auction Day
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. At the auction, Ulyana publicly reads the translated sentence instead of bidding, forfeiting the house and exposing the family myth before strangers and developer alike. Vivienne wins the lot, then falters. Emotional beat: catharsis through public ruin; truth costs more than money and buys less.

chapters.title: Return Address
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV, weeks later. The last bus to the old neighborhood makes its final run; he rides it beside Vivienne, who has decided to build something small and honest on the lot rather than sell. He mails one last postcard—to himself, with a return address. Emotional beat: resolution without absolution; inheritance redefined as what you choose to carry forward.
